text: Post-harvest handling for a seed crop is stricter than for ordinary paddy, because every step affects germination. Harvest timing: wait until about 90% of the grains in the field have turned golden/straw-colored before cutting - a higher maturity threshold than for regular paddy, since fully mature, well-filled grain germinates best. Harvest method: hand harvesting with a sickle is preferred for seed production, because it causes far less shattering, cracking, and impact damage to the seed coat than machine harvesting, and lowers the risk of accidentally mixing in grain from a different variety nearby. Machine (combine) harvesting is faster and cheaper, but causes more impact damage and shattering loss; if a combine must be used for a seed lot, discard the first 2-3 loads of threshed grain that come out (likely still mixed with residue from whatever field the machine worked before), and only keep grain threshed after that. Threshing: hand-beating or foot-treading is preferred over stick-threshing or machine threshing, since it causes less friction and impact damage to the seed coat; where machine threshing can't be avoided, feed small amounts by hand at a time to reduce impact damage. Sun-drying: dry immediately after threshing to preserve grain brightness and quality. Spread seed out in batches and cover it during the hottest sun hours (around 12:00-1:00 pm), then uncover to keep drying as the afternoon heat eases; never sun-dry more than one seed lot side by side without clear separation, since chickens, wind, or children playing nearby can mix seed lots together. A flat-bed mechanical dryer is an alternative for larger seed volumes and avoids the labor of sun-drying, but temperature must be carefully controlled to avoid overheating the grain; target storage moisture is 12-14%. Cleaning: winnow with wind, a hand fan, or a winnowing/blower device to remove empty grains, soil, chaff, and other debris. Packaging and storage: pack cleaned, dried seed into sacks and machine-stitch the seams closed; store in a dedicated dry, well-ventilated room with a roof and sealed walls that keep out rain and rodents; keep storage moisture under about 13-14%; and stack sacks in rows on wooden pallets or brick/concrete blocks so they never sit directly on a soil floor.
